title: Calibrate directional-pair tests under sparse and concentrated vocabulary
statement: For 20 independently seeded 5,000-token books in each cell, five-type cycles never reject either shuffle null at p <= .05, while 20-, 100- and 500-type cycles reject in all 20 trials under both gap rules. Corresponding iid books reject in 0–2 of 20 trials per condition. Mean observed skew-type fraction under iid falls from .78–.85 at five types to zero at 500, illustrating that the fixed threshold changes behavior greatly with vocabulary size. The samples and processes are limited and are not general power or type-I error estimates.
check: Extend the partially completed P-J-037 calibration to unequal-frequency and tied-frequency alphabets, other stationary and nonstationary transition processes, deterministic substitutions, realistic noisy and planted ciphers, independent historical books and page-clustered nulls; quantify uncertainty across independent texts and prespecify rules before manuscript evaluation.
methods: Each synthetic book has 5,000 tokens, partitioned into blocks of 80 (last 40). A cycle advances through a vocabulary of V tokens with independent random block phase; iid draws uniformly from V tokens. V = 5, 20, 100, 500. Twenty seeds per cell. Most frequent type is removed, ties broken lexicographically. Measure unequal directed pairs at forward distances 1–3 within blocks, and fraction of observed unordered pair types with absolute count imbalance > 5. Compare the original with 99 independent within-block token shuffles using one-sided add-one p <= .05. Two policies separately compress removed tokens or treat them as barriers. Seeds are deterministic; see script. The plan extends the exploratory P-J-031 measure, not an external preregistration.
limitations: Cycles are deliberately regular nonlanguage controls, and iid books are exchangeable by construction. Twenty runs give wide uncertainty; rows and gap policies are correlated. Lexical tie-breaking is not substitution invariant. The selected vocabulary sizes do not independently model manuscript page distributions. No historical input or manuscript evaluation is used here; this addresses only part of the requested calibration.
